cards.context: 全球变暖背景下，海洋吸收了人类活动产生的约90%多余热量，海温逐年攀升。此次连续100天破纪录发生在厄尔尼诺正在发展的背景下，意味着自然气候波动与人为变暖叠加，可能将海洋温度推向更极端的水平。

cards.source_text: - Data indicates that the global ocean sustained 100 consecutive days of record heat between June 2 and Sept. 10, and the high sea surface temperatures don’t give any indications of dropping in the near future. - Experts attribute this episode to climate change, which they say the current El Niño weather pattern is amplifying. - The record-breaking ocean heat has drawn concerns from experts about the effects on marine ecosystems, global weather patterns, and economies that depend on the ocean. For 100 consecutive days between June 2 and Sept. 10, the global ocean outside of polar regions sustained record high average sea surface temperatures, according to data from the Climate Reanalyzer, a platform overseen by the University of Maine’s Climate Change Institute in the U.S. On each of the 100 days, sea surface temperatures exceeded those on the same date in every other year on record since 1982. One of the highest readings occurred on Aug. 22, when global ocean sea surface temperatures reached 21.10° Celsius (69.98° Fahrenheit), according to the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service. The Climate Reanalyzer reported temperatures climbing even higher between Aug. 22 and 27, with average ocean sea surface temperatures hitting 21.18° C (70.12° F). The platform draws on global sea surface temperature data recorded by the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). These record temperatures are likely to remain elevated in the near future “given the state of the intensifying El Niño,” said Zachary Labe, a climate scientist at the U.S.-based nonprofit Climate Central, which communicates climate change science. In a Sept. 10 press briefing that discussed the Climate Reanalyzer data, Labe said this record ocean heat is part of a long-term trend driven by the human-induced climate crisis. Without a reduction in greenhouse gases, he said the oceans will continue to warm. “The driver of this record warmth is climate change,” he said, “and more than 90% of that excess heat from burning fossil fuels and those greenhouse gas emissions goes into the ocean.” Experts say the unprecedented ocean heat is affecting marine ecosystems, global weather patterns, and economies that depend on the ocean for food security, livelihoods and coastal protection. Indra Kurnia, director of conservation at the Sumatran Orangutan Lestari Foundation–Orangutan Information Center (YOSL-OIC). The five youngsters were found on Sept. 8 by locals near the Bichitrapur forest area in Balasore district, Odisha, a state on India’s east coast formed out of the ancient Kalinga region. cards.relevant: 黑洞“遗忘”历史信息的现象与物理学中著名的“黑洞信息悖论”密切相关，触及量子力学与广义相对论的根本矛盾，是理论物理最前沿的难题之一。
cards.context: 当两个黑洞合并时，会产生引力波信号，新黑洞先经历剧烈振动（ringdown），然后迅速稳定。根据“无毛定理”，最终的黑洞只由质量、电荷和自旋三个参数描述，几乎不保留合并前的任何细节信息。

The bells of Great St Mary’s church play the familiar melody of the Cambridge Quarters. The sound, now often associated with the chimes of Big Ben in London, was first composed here in 1793. The quarters, named for the melody at each quarter-hour, are an immediately recognisable reminder of the passage of time. Each bell produces a note: a wave with a characteristic frequency that travels through the air and reaches our ears. A hammer strikes the bell, and it oscillates, pushing air molecules back and forth. Those jostling molecules reach our ears and we hear a musical note. Then the bell settles, gives up its energy, and returns to silence. My research here at the University of Cambridge often brings me back to the ringing of a bell. I don’t study the physics of sound, but I do focus on a remarkably similar process, taking place throughout the Universe. I am interested in another object that also rings: a black hole. As I sit down with a coffee, I open my laptop to a wavy signal that gradually fades to a flat line. Two black holes have finished merging – a frenzied process of coalescence – leaving an extremely brief wiggle originating from the remnant black hole. Much like the struck bell, this leftover black hole is ringing in a process called ringdown, and it’s consistent across every merger I investigate. Ringdown allows physicists to test their theories of gravity: did Albert Einstein really have the last word? Just as an off-sounding note from a bell might indicate a design flaw, a discrepancy in the frequencies of a ringing black hole could be the first crack in our understanding of gravity. That’s the scientific rationale for studying ringdown, but what fascinates me equally is what happens next. After the black hole rings, it settles into silence. In that moment, lasting only a few milliseconds, the power and intensity of the merger are lost. From the exterior, almost all of that history suddenly becomes inaccessible, and what is left is featureless. The black hole settles into a simple, peaceful object of pure spacetime, with no trace of the violence that just happened. In some respects, the black holes forget. It seems counterintuitive that something so chaotically created can become so simple. Why do black holes seem to forget their violent histories? cards.source_text: Anslem de Silva is widely regarded as the father of modern herpetology in Sri Lanka. He has spent more than six decades documenting the island’s rich reptile and amphibian diversity while mentoring generations of researchers. De Silva spoke with Mongabay contributor Malaka Rodrigo as he, at 86 years old, prepares to host the first World Congress on Snakes. The conference in October in Sri Lanka’s hill city of Kandy will be an international gathering specifically dedicated to snake conservation and research. Over the course of a distinguished career, de Silva has authored more than 350 scientific papers and more than 25 books. His work began in the 1960s when only a small handful of Sri Lankan researchers were studying the country’s reptiles and amphibians. To build local scientific capacity, he organized the country’s first one-day herpetological conference in the 1960s. He also launched Sri Lanka’s first herpetological research journal, Lyriocephalus, and established the Amphibia and Reptile Research Organization of Sri Lanka in 1990. De Silva’s mentorship has left a lasting legacy across the region. Ruchira Somaweera, a Sri Lankan-born conservation biologist, recalled receiving an inscribed copy of the journal from de Silva when he was just 13. “Most of the herpetologists of my generation were groomed by de Silva, and hundreds, if not thousands, of students have been inspired by him, just like I was,” Somaweera told Mongabay. Born in 1940 in the southern coastal city of Matara, de Silva developed his passion for snakes as a child after rescuing a rat snake (Ptyas mucosa) that was being abused by other students. Before becoming a leading scientist, he was an accomplished magician who won the national title of Best Magician in 1965. He credits magic with honing his public communication skills. “Communicating the value of conservation to the public is an art; a matter of good storytelling,” de Silva, who currently serves as co-chair of the IUCN Amphibian Specialist Group, told Rodrigo. “I believe my experience as a magician helped me to reveal the true magicians of nature — reptiles and amphibians.” A key priority for de Silva is countering public fear and misperceptions about snakes. While Sri Lanka is home to more than 100 snake species, only about five species can cause fatal bites, according to de Silva. cards.source_text: Frank Lloyd Wright was often strapped for cash. In that respect, he had something in common with Vincent van Gogh, who passed most of his much shorter life in more dire circumstances. Unlike Wright, who enjoyed decades of fame at the pinnacle of the American architectural profession, van Gogh remained practically unknown until after his death. But if they’ve encountered one another in the afterlife, they’ve certainly discussed one subject above all others: their shared appreciation for Japanese woodblock prints. Here on Open Culture, we’ve previously featured the collection of 500 such works of art that van Gogh left behind. At the end of Wright’s life in 1959, he owned about 6,000, many of which his estate had to sell to pay both Japanese art dealers and American tax collectors. We could say that Wright died as he lived, advanced age having not evidently diminished either his financial recklessness or his obsession with ukiyo‑e. The masters of that classical “art of the floating world” like Hokusai and Hiroshige were among his favorite artists of any kind. It isn’t certain how well the young Wright knew Fenollosa — or indeed when he began collecting ukiyo‑e, writes Frank Lloyd Wright and the Art of Japan author Julia Meech-Pekarik, though he may have seen both Hokusai and Hiroshige’s works at the World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893, “about the time he opened his practice in Oak Park.” Eight years later, “Wright made his first voyage to Japan in pursuit of prints, and he did indeed return with enough expertise to stage an exhibition of his own Hiroshige collection at the Art Institute of Chicago in March of 1906.” He returned for two months in 1913, making it clear that he was only interested in using that time to acquire more prints. cards.relevant: 《Jugend》杂志是研究德国新艺术运动和20世纪初欧洲视觉文化的重要原始资料，其停刊也折射出纳粹时期文化管控的历史。
cards.context: 《Jugend》创刊于1896年，以推广新艺术风格为宗旨，对德国现代设计和视觉文化影响深远。1933年纳粹推行Gleichschaltung政策后，媒体和文化出版受到严格管控，该杂志最终于1940年停刊。
cards.source_analysis: Open Culture聚合免费文化资源，常推荐可下载的历史文献和艺术作品。
cards.source_text: It’s an ungainly word for English speakers, which is maybe why we do not hear it often: Gleichschaltung. Yet the concept remains central for a clear view of what happened to Germany in the 1930s. In 1933, the nation completely transformed, seemingly overnight, through “a concerted policy of ‘coordination’ (Gleichschaltung),” the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum writes. “Culture, the economy, education, and law all came under Nazi control.” Those artists and organizations that were not purged had their essential character changed to reflect an entirely different set of artistic and political values. One publication, especially, serves as an example of the Nazification of culture. The arts journal Jugend (Youth), writes Messy Nessy Chic, “had been turned largely into propaganda” between 1933 and 1940, its final year. But prior to the regime’s takeover, Jugend showcased the most avant-garde, “degenerate” artists of the era, and might have been “the ‘brainiest’ periodical of the day,” as one critic wrote in a 1904 issue of The Yale Literary Magazine. “There is no magazine published in England or in this country which is at all like it.” You can take a look yourself—browse, search, and download hundreds of scanned issues of Jugend at the University of Heidelberg’s digital archive, thousands of pages in PDF form, spanning the magazine’s forty-four-year history. You can also see images at Flickr. As in England, France, Austria, and the U.S., the Art Nouveau movement in Germany emerged from a whirlwind of post-Impressionist painting, Orientalist motifs, folk art, modernist art and advertising, book illustration, and graphic and industrial design. Appropriately, given its perch on the threshold of a new century, Art Nouveau looked both backward—to the medieval, gothic, and Romantic—and forward toward a more modernist, urbane, and urbanized sensibility. So influential was Jugend that Art Nouveau in Germany became known as Jugendstil. The Oxford Critical and Cultural History of Modernist Magazines writes, “Among Jugend’s most important qualities—indeed, an essential aspect of Art Nouveau and its German equivalent Jugendstil—was its brilliant escapism.” Founded in 1896 by writer Georg Hirth, the magazine was “from the start a venue to promote the new cultural Renaissance without recourse to the established ‘vintage’ art.” (See its very first cover right above.) cards.source_text: To what extent can we ever understand the experiences of nonhuman animals? And to what extent do we even understand our own? These questions sit at the heart of the short poetic documentary Animal Eye, which probes the diverse visual worlds of creatures big and small. For the film, the US director Carlo Nasisse pairs the reflections of philosophers and scientists with ruminative in-the-lab images of a wide range of animals. Starting from the biology, beauty and mystery of the eye, Nasisse constructs a broader exploration of the limits of human understanding, and our drive to keep looking regardless. cards.source_text: Mahmoud Khalil was completing a master’s degree at Columbia University when, in March 2025, plain-clothed officers from the Department of Homeland Security snatched him from his home in New York and took him to an immigration detention centre; he was then transferred to another facility in Louisiana, more than 1,000 miles away. As a green card holder, Khalil has permanent US residency, but secretary of state Marco Rubio had determined that his continued presence in the country would have “adverse foreign policy consequences for the United States”, and sought his deportation under a legal provision dating back to the McCarthy era. Khalil was released on bail in June 2024 after a federal judge ruled his detention unconstitutional, but the Trump administration is still trying to have him removed. Khalil – who was born to Palestinian parents in a refugee camp in Syria – had been targeted because of his advocacy on behalf of pro-Palestinian protesters during campus protests over Columbia University’s links to Israel. They were calling for Columbia to cut its ties with Israeli academic institutions and companies profiting from Israel’s onslaught on Gaza; in response, the university called in the NYPD. There was no suggestion that Khalil had done anything unlawful, and no criminal charges were brought against him; the government had simply identified him as an influential pro-Palestinian voice on campus, and for that reason alone they wanted him gone. He spent a total of 104 days in detention, missing the birth of his son. Khalil recounts this Kafkaesque ordeal with a quiet fury in his memoir, No Land to Stand On. The episode is a damning snapshot of the Trump administration’s creeping authoritarianism and the cruelty of its immigration enforcement policy. Khalil was a high-profile detainee whose case drew considerable public scrutiny; he had access to lawyers, and was eventually able to extricate himself. Many of his fellow prisoners at the facility, hailing from places as diverse as Georgia, Romania, Senegal, Nepal, El Salvador and Chechnya, were less fortunate. They languish in detention for months on end, at the mercy of an opaque and glacially slow legal bureaucracy, “forgotten in a system designed to forget them”. cards.source_text: Eliza Griffiths was at home in New York, drinking a second cup of coffee one August morning in 2022, when her phone rang. She answered it to a frantic friend, who told her the man she had married just a year earlier, and who had set off the previous night for a speaking engagement nearly 400 miles away, had been hurt. “What kind of hurt?” she panicked. Turning on the television, she was assaulted by blurry images of chaos on stage as audience members surged to the rescue. Her husband, Sir Salman Rushdie, had been stabbed multiple times and was fighting for his life. Within days of desperately chartering a plane to fly her to Rushdie’s hospital bedside, not knowing if he was alive or dead, Griffiths – a poet and photographer who works under her full name Rachel Eliza Griffiths – had begun to make a video diary recording his treatment and recovery. “When it had become likely that I was going to survive,” says Rushdie drily, “I said to Eliza we need to make a record of this. By which I meant something very modest: maybe she would take a picture of me on her iPhone every couple of days just to document the recovery, but Eliza had bigger ideas.” One of her first ideas was that it needed to be shot not on a phone but with a proper camera. “I explicitly remember when the box arrived with my camera,” Griffiths says. “I cried because it was reconnecting me to my identity as an artist. The person I used to be, even just 24 hours ago, was being returned to me. It was giving both of us this permission to continue to be artists and tell our stories together.” The couple are sitting in separate rooms of their New York home to tell their shared story over video link. Griffiths is warm and animated, as the memories rush out. Rushdie is more reserved and sardonic, smartly turned out, with only a black lens over his right eye to attest to the horrific injuries he suffered. Both have already published memoirs about the experience: Rushdie’s Knife, in 2024 and Griffiths’ The Flower Bearers earlier this year. Now they are the subjects of an unflinching film, Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie, which combines Griffiths’ video diary with archive footage from the period following the fateful day in 1989 when a fatwa was issued against Rushdie for the offence allegedly caused to Islam by the supposed blasphemy of his fourth novel, The Satanic Verses. The room was packed full of appliances, as if a commercial kitchen had been blown apart. Several stacks of wall ovens huddled together on dollies. Tangles of electrical cords popped up behind a broad stainless-steel counter. Rags and sponges dried slowly on the edge of a giant sink, over which a pre-rinse nozzle drooped like a willow branch. Nearby, a computer monitor showed Python developer tools next to a spreadsheet dotted with red and green cells. In the middle of the room was an improvised prep station on which there was an odd little machine. It looked like a tiny microwave designed to warm up a single cupcake. I later learned it’s a moisture analyser: the researchers use it to see how much juice is left in their samples of lamb, swordfish, chicken, pork and beef. I’m writing down everything I see: 10:45 am. The kitchen is full of smoke. That basement room was a test kitchen, where two chefs and several researchers had been busy cooking a whole farm’s worth of meat in a set of prototype ovens. The company’s vision was to invent a cooking machine that could whip up Michelin-grade dishes at the press of a button, and the crew was tasting the food and filling out ‘sensory inventory’ forms that recorded qualities like colour, smell, temperature, texture and taste. As the design lead for the oven’s touchscreen interface, I was there to learn from the chefs in order to build something that worked for them and for the ‘home chef’ or end user. The tension between their culinary intuition and the ovens’ logic was immediately apparent: the kitchen was full of smoke because one chef had attempted to cook three racks of lamb directly under a broiler to get the colour you’d get by ‘smacking it with a propane torch’. This instinct didn’t translate to a language the oven understood. I wrote down Smacking? and kept watching. The other chef, tapping away on another of the ovens’ screens, muttered: ‘These things are worthless. I need to be able to use my chef spidey senses.’ The chefs were hired to help program the ovens to follow their recipes. But they also had to pretend they were normal people cooking dinner for their families in order to see if the ovens could replicate expert techniques. cards.source_text: Derek Gow and Derek Banbury should hate each other. Gow is an outspoken rewilder widely credited with bringing back the beaver in England. As he returns his Devon sheep farm to wild nature, he is also breeding storks, wildcats, red-backed shrikes, glowworms and even adders to return to the countryside. Over the hedge, Banbury, his neighbour, is proud to be an intensive farmer, producing milk and beef cattle behind tightly clipped hedges. “It’s like he’s just gone mad,” says Banbury of Gow at the start of Derek vs Derek, an illuminating and unexpectedly funny new documentary that follows the pair over three years. “And the madness is now crossing the road on to my land.” What begins as a portrait of neighbours at war, with no hope of bridging the chasm between modern chemical farmers and idealistic rewilders, or between the needs of food production and the worsening extinction crisis, is slowly and subtly upended, as the two Dereks learn to live alongside each other and hopeful seeds of common ground are sown. Documentary-maker James Dawson started following Gow as he sold the last of his sheep, planning a film about the dramatic changes brought about by rewilding his farm. Then, when Dawson first visited Gow, he was put up at the Banburys, where wife Linda has turned former pigsties and old sheds into holiday cottages. As soon as Dawson met Derek Banbury over breakfast in the farmhouse kitchen, he knew he had to make a rather different film. As well as a boundary, both Dereks share a certain charisma, bloody-mindedness, business acumen and, actually, a love of animals. Gow is an imposing, fast-talking, sweary Scot who criticises “showers of morons” in conservation for convening endless committees while species plummet towards extinction. He’s equally disdainful of farmers “spaffing” public money on Land Rovers and sticking sheep on overgrazed pastures and feeding them fish-meal from the Gambia, “raping what’s left of a disastrous environment to produce something that nobody wants”. Meanwhile, Banbury, who has an impish grin and quick wit, is unrepentant about agribusiness. “I love farming,” he declares in the film. “Intensive farming, that’s supplying the world with food. The population’s getting bigger. It’s not getting smaller, and everyone is going to be happy if they’ve got full bellies. I’ve done it for 50 years and I won’t change. I won’t change.” Or will he? cards.source_text: Louisiana firefighters responding to a small house blaze found a wildcat native to sub-Saharan Africa illegally enclosed in the back yard, and an animal welfare agency is now seeking to place the creature in an appropriate environment, according to officials. Firefighters investigating a report of a minor fire at a home in the suburban New Orleans community of Marrero on Tuesday spotted the cat in question – an African serval – behind the residence in a chain-linked enclosure resembling a cramped baseball batting cage, a spokesperson for the local animal protection services said. A statement from Jefferson protection and animal welfare services (JPaws) said its director, Michelle Brignac, and humane department supervisor, Victoria Clark, joined firefighters at the scene after they were summoned there. Local laws require an exotic animal permit to legally keep a serval as a pet, and the owner of the home at the center of the case did not have such a document, JPaws spokesperson John McCusker told the Guardian on Thursday. The statement said Brignac and Clark therefore “subdued the hissing serval and wrangled it” into a transport carrier from its 9ft-by-9ft (7.53-sq-meter) cage that McCusker likened to “a dog kennel”. Brignac and Clark then brought the serval to the JPaws facility in the nearby community of Harvey, according to the statement from the agency, which also shared vivid photographs of the wildcat. Beside their black spots, svelte physiques and striking facial features, servals are known for their ability to leap as high as about 7ft (2 meters) in the air. So McCusker said JPaws gave the serval an entire room to itself while the agency sought an appropriate refuge for the wildcat, which was born in captivity but whose natural habitat is African grasslands. Servals share some similarities with domesticated cats that make them immensely popular as pets, including their affinities for grooming themselves, purring, yowling and stalking potential prey. Nonetheless, they are not easily sustained pets, JPaws’ statement maintained. Servals in captivity do not have the physical space and stimulation needed to engage in normal, healthy behaviors, and they endure chronic stress as a result, the agency’s statement said. They mark their territory, become aggressive as they mature, cannot be fully house-trained and destroy furniture, and they have been known to barge through walls and doors, according to JPaws. A year after the Canadian pop star released her breakthrough record, 2015’s E•MO•TION, she returned with E•MO•TION Side B. 2019’s Dedicated received similar treatment. By the time Jepsen released the companion album to 2022’s The Loneliest Time, the “surprise” drop hardly registered. This brand of excess is key to Jepsen’s charm. Here is a singer who’ll repeat the word “really” six times in a row in a song’s chorus, just to make sure you really get the message; who claimed she wrote 200 songs for one 12-track record, then another hundred for her next one. Her latest album, Day and Night, tweaks her formula of abundance slightly, offering—in a CRJ first—a full double album upfront. As its title suggests, the record comprises two distinct themes: sweet, sunny tracks for Day; sleeker, dancier songs for Night. Working with a familiar stable of producers and co-writers, she turns out a sprawling album filled with loose, breezy tracks offset by the occasional pop gem and charming left-field details. No score yet, be the first to add. Day hews mostly to the windswept ballads and disco-inflected pop that Jepsen moved toward on her previous set of records: “After All” and “Something Tragic” are lightly psychedelic, her voice all breathy and urgent; there’s a little chillwave on “Habits of Creatures,” a little folk on “Wild Child.” Night is more strictly synth-pop: “Don’t Leave Me on the Dancefloor” is the cleanest ABBA homage she’s ever managed, and I wouldn’t have been surprised to hear the ultra-yearning “That’s Just Me” as a deep-cut E•MO•TION castoff. Day and Night’s sprawl is a double-edged sword. Though the production is usually layered and finely detailed, most songs don’t contain the razor-sharp hooks that usually make Jepsen’s work so indelible. In their absence, each side becomes a little unwieldy, and both Day and Night sag in their second halves. Only a fool would doubt that the prolific Jepsen could write 24 full tracks for a vaguely conceptual double album—but one wonders if a more focused, refined concept would better sustain its momentum. But perhaps a pared-back version of this record wouldn’t allow for the strange, quasi-experimental detours that populate it. cards.source_text: Last year, the fashion writer Biz Sherbert went to a Deftones concert in Atlanta and interviewed attendees before the show. The 2020s revitalization of the alt-metal pioneers is pretty well established at this point, but Sherbert’s documentation showed off the band’s popularity with young women specifically; she photographed teenagers and college students in miniskirts and tank tops, many of whom had discovered Deftones algorithmically, through Spotify or TikTok. The scene looked a lot different than the one I remember from seeing the band in 2003 in a sea of black-clad nu-metal bros. One group of young women even called Deftones a “girl band,” exclaiming, “This is girly pop music!” So when Deftones vocalist Chino Moreno shows up to do backing vocals for the last track of Beabadoobee’s latest album, it makes all the sense in the world, Beatrice Laus, currently 26 years old, has made her share of music that could be called “girly pop,” but with her fourth studio album, Pylon, she threads the needle between her usual brand of sweet-but-melancholic pop rock, and a newer, rougher sound. The ingredients that gave 2024’s This Is How Tomorrow Moves its darling tweeness—peppy horns, tender piano—have been replaced with elements that will please anyone who spent their adolescence learning how to professionally glower: tapped harmonics, twirly twin guitar loops, sludgy riffs, screeching feedback. It’s a reverse Sour Patch Kid situation—first Beabadoobee was sweet, now she’s getting sour. No score yet, be the first to add. To solidify the vibe shift, Laus has tapped an impressive breadth of alt-rock stars from the past couple of decades. Besides Moreno, we get vocals from Hayley Williams, guitar and songwriting contributions from Title Fight’s Shane Moran, one song co-written with Evan Stevens Hall from Pinegrove (one of Laus’s favorite bands, to the point of her getting a Pinegrove neck tattoo last year), and an appearance from Turnstile’s Brendan Yates so dour that, at first listen, I thought he was Bladee. Often, just two out of three of these requirements did the trick. It worked for Gracie Abrams, Olivia Rodrigo, and even briefly for Katie Gregson-MacLeod, of “complex” fame. That formula also helped Lizzy McAlpine—a singer-songwriter from Pennsylvania who first garnered attention on social media while a student at Berklee College of Music, uploading videos from home when the pandemic shut down school. Then, her 2022 ballad “Ceilings” sparked a TikTok trend in which people ran away from the camera and passionately belted out its confessional lyrics. The viral success of “Ceilings” epitomized how McAlpine’s early music felt built for a romantic comedy: first swooning, then devastation in the third act. But for her fourth album, Angel, she takes a more homespun approach. McAlpine sounds less like a heroine of a coming-of-age film than a songwriter at an open mic, testing out material for an audience primed to turn songs into snippets. No score yet, be the first to add. Before her third studio album, Older, McAlpine parted ways with producers Philip Etherington and Ehren Ebbage, who were responsible for some of her early hits and had a more cinematic pop flair. Instead, she began working with a live band, making secular songs reminiscent of contemporary worship music. It’s not necessarily the subject matter of songs like “Spring Into Summer” or “Pushing It Down and Praying”; it’s their swelling arrangements, and the fact that McAlpine has a velvety voice fit for a youth worship leader. She continues that trend on Angel. cards.source_text: Just when you thought the kids had buried the Beatles for good, here’s AKRIILA with lucy miró al mundo y notó que está girando. The title of the rising Chilean star’s new album (“Lucy looked at the world and noticed it’s turning”) borrows lines from “While My Guitar Gently Weeps” and “Lucy in the Sky With Diamonds,” the first song AKRIILA learned to play on the piano. The Fab Four might seem like an unlikely reference point for a flame-haired 22-year-old whose berserk debut album was filled with robotic tags like “Hot gays listen to AKRIILA” and “Hot twinks listen to AKRIILA.” But the more you listen, the more it makes a weird kind of sense. AKRIILA makes omnivorous music, the byproduct of a peripatetic appetite and an inability or refusal to streamline her impulses. She doesn’t sound like the Beatles; she sounds like someone playing you her 10 favorite records at the same time, a charming mash of dog-eared pages and favorited tabs. Akri’s Lucy is not Julian Lennon’s classmate Lucy, nor LSD, nor a love interest. It's a protagonist learning to live alone in a grown-up, lovesick world—and also, separately, a snail. Snails are pathetic, precious things, locomoting calmly as chaos erupts around them. On the album cover, AKRIILA holds a snail named Lucy as light breaks in from every side. As lucy unfolds, the record moves from the bitter depths of heartbreak to something like acceptance, or the painful death that’s necessary for the light to eventually come back. On the trip-hoppy, dream-poppy second track, “moriría y moriría” (“I would die and die”), AKRIILA threatens to shoot herself if she can’t have her sweetheart. Fast forward to the languorous ache of closer “lucy,” where AKRIILA sees a snail that’s sure to die, and she gives up; she says the world has stopped turning. “Ya no sé por qué aún me esfuerzo,” (“I don’t know why I still try”), she sighs. No score yet, be the first to add. While the album is packed with these love-scarred lyrics and angsty entreaties, you wouldn’t know it from the production, which is mostly handled by longtime collaborators Heartgaze and Vinco. Where AKRIILA’s 2024 album epistolares turbocharged Nia Archives’ sensitive jungle for a neoperreo club night, lucy uses mad thuds and speedy rhythms sparingly, saving a “Think” break for a sick flash on “un <3 inestable.” The new sound is groovy guitars and drums that make being down bad sound like springtime bliss, like crying and smiling while watching the sunrise say hiii. cards.source_text: As Jawdropped tell it, Los Angeles isn’t such a bad home for aspiring musicians. Practice spaces are generally easy to come by. Transporting gear to the gig is no problem—you’re already used to sitting in your car all the time. For every DIY venue that shutters, there’s a new one ready to pop in another neighborhood just a touch less gentrified. And most importantly, cutting your teeth in such a sprawling creative hotbed means there’s a good chance of crossing paths with likeminded people who each have their own complicated feelings about what it means to “make it.” That creative hotbed is where Jawdropped met, anyway, and its characters serve as the nexus for the quartet’s debut album, Secret to Spare. Vocalist Kyra Morling, vocalist/guitarist Roman Zangari, bassist Sean Edwards, and drummer Cook Lee-Chobanian are longtime Angelenos who, all in their 30s, have accumulated plenty of experience across a slew projects that never quite took off. They formed Jawdropped a little over two years ago, solidifying their early friendship by attending an Evan Dando show together and exploring crunchy power-pop of their own on their 2025 EP, Just Fantasy. But the Lemonheads’ influence becomes even clearer on Secret to Spare, as early as the first ten seconds of opener “The Line,” where Morling counts off a rush of sunny, major-key guitar chords that feel lifted straight from It’s a Shame About Ray. No score yet, be the first to add. But where Dando’s narrators were often disaffected or passive, Jawdropped pride themselves on wearing their hearts as blatantly as their influences on their sleeves. They’re far from their generation’s first band to namecheck Paul Westerberg, Teenage Fanclub, and Dinosaur Jr. in one breath, but there’s a refreshing sincerity to their ’90s revivalism: “I’m just not interested in coming off mysterious or cool,” Zangari has said, distinguishing himself from the myriad zoomers who made cribbing Deftones fashionable. “Monday,” a pop-punkish early single about overcoming hesitance toward telling somebody how you really feel, forges some transparent urgency: ”If I wait one more day/I might go insane/Cause I’m just wasting time,” Morling and Zangari sing in unison, their overlapping vocals lending a bar-band warmth to their self-produced fidelity. Across Secret to Spare, Jawdropped couch these interpersonal, observational stories in the trepidations of the big-city grind. items.summary: The Palestinian Columbia student snatched by ICE writes about his Kafkaesque ordeal with a quiet fury Mahmoud Khalil was completing a master’s degree at Columbia University when, in March 2025, plain-clothed officers from the Department of Homeland Security snatched him from his home in New York and took him to an immigration detention centre; he was then transferred to another facility in Louisiana, more than 1,000 miles away. As a green card holder, Khalil has permanent US residency, but secretary of state Marco Rubio had determined that his continued presence in the country would have “adverse foreign policy consequences for the United States”, and sought his deportation under a legal provision dating back to the McCarthy era. Khalil was released on bail in June 2024 after a federal judge ruled his detention unconstitutional, but the Trump administration is still trying to have him removed. Khalil – who was born to Palestinian parents in a refugee camp in Syria – had been targeted because of his advocacy on behalf of pro-Palestinian protesters during campus protests over Columbia University’s links to Israel. They were calling for Columbia to cut its ties with Israeli academic institutions and companies profiting from Israel’s onslaught on Gaza; in response, the university called in the NYPD. There was no suggestion that Khalil had done anything unlawful, and no criminal charges were brought against him; the government had simply identified him as an influential pro-Palestinian voice on campus, and for that reason alone they wanted him gone. He spent a total of 104 days in detention, missing the birth of his son. Continue reading...

items.summary: After ​the writer was stabbed in a horrific attack, his wife started making a video diary of his recovery. The clips are featured in a new film from Alex Gibney, who drew on Dennis Potter to create a powerful portrait of Rushdie’s tumultuous life Eliza Griffiths was at home in New York, drinking a second cup of coffee one August morning in 2022, when her phone rang. She answered it to a frantic friend, who told her the man she had married just a year earlier, and who had set off the previous night for a speaking engagement nearly 400 miles away, had been hurt. “What kind of hurt?” she panicked. Turning on the television, she was assaulted by blurry images of chaos on stage as audience members surged to the rescue. Her husband, Sir Salman Rushdie, had been stabbed multiple times and was fighting for his life. Within days of desperately chartering a plane to fly her to Rushdie’s hospital bedside, not knowing if he was alive or dead, Griffiths – a poet and photographer who works under her full name Rachel Eliza Griffiths – had begun to make a video diary recording his treatment and recovery. “When it had become likely that I was going to survive,” says Rushdie drily, “I said to Eliza we need to make a record of this. By which I meant something very modest: maybe she would take a picture of me on her iPhone every couple of days just to document the recovery, but Eliza had bigger ideas.” Continue reading...
